en: Treatise on the Non-Existence of External Objects (*Nirālambanavāda*) Composed by the Bodhisattva Dignāga Translated by the Tripitaka Master Paramārtha of Western India from the Chen Dynasty.
If one speaks of atoms (*paramāṇu*), they are the fundamental cause; because [the cognition] arises without resembling them, they are not the object, just as the sense organs are not.
Consciousness arises resembling an aggregate, yet it does not arise from that [aggregate]; the aggregate has no substantial reality, just like a second moon.
Based on these two meanings, external objects are not [direct] sense-fields (*viṣaya*).
Some say that atoms (*paramāṇu*) aggregate to form the myriad things; since consciousness arises appearing as their likeness, they are established as sense-fields.
If the essential characteristic of the atom (*paramāṇu*) were substantially existent, then because consciousness does not resemble it, it would not be an object, unlike gross matter.
If the atom were like gross matter, then consciousness would have no distinction;
if one says their characteristics differ, then consciousness would not be uniform.

Diverse characteristics exist only in the conventional; therefore, their substance is not real. As for the dimensions of the atoms (*paramāṇu*), there is no distinction among them in their various locations.
If these atoms were removed, the myriad consciousnesses would not arise; therefore, all things are entirely mere designations (*prajñapti*).
The internal objective aspect appears as if it were external; it is established as the object-field of consciousness because consciousness manifests in its likeness.
A common functional capacity is established to cause [the aspects] to arise in succession; thus, the two faculties arise together.
Superior capacity constitutes the root;
it is unimpeded within consciousness. They act as causes for one another, with superior capacity serving as the object-field; they arise mutually from time without beginning.

If there are those who maintain that the six consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, arise by taking external objects as their conditions, such persons must either take atoms (*paramāṇu*) as the object because they are the cause of that consciousness,
or take a collection of atoms as the object because the consciousness arises appearing as a collection.
What is the characteristic of an object (*viṣaya*)?

If consciousness can discern its essential nature and characteristics, and if consciousness arises in accordance with that essential nature and those characteristics, for this reason it is called an "object.
An atom (*paramāṇu*) does not possess this quality.
If atoms were truly the cause of consciousness, as for example the five sense organs are, then atoms would not be objects.
If that were so, a collection of atoms should be the object, because consciousness arises with respect to the collection.
Even though this is so, consciousness does not arise from that [collection] in accordance with its characteristics; therefore, the collection is also not an object (*viṣaya*). Why is this?
If an object could produce consciousness such that it resembles the object's own essence and characteristics, then it could be accepted as an object.
Why is this? Because it can be said that these atoms serve as the conditions for the arising of consciousness.
A collection, however, is not like this, because it does not exist substantially.

For example, when the eye faculty is impaired, a consciousness arises that perceives two moons; yet these two moons are not the objective domain of that consciousness, because they do not exist in reality.
A composite aggregate (*saṃcita*) is likewise: since it lacks any substantial entity apart from its atoms (*paramāṇu*), the aggregate is not the objective domain of consciousness.
Therefore, external objects are not the objective domain of consciousness by virtue of these two meanings, because each individual atom lacks them.

Some masters say: "The aggregation of atoms constitutes the myriad things; since they possess a multitude of characteristics in their entirety, this [aggregation] is established as the objective domain."

Why is this? There exists a distinct characteristic capable of producing realized wisdom (*pramāṇa-jñāna*), which is not merely the atom (*paramāṇu*) or the aggregate of atoms (*paramāṇu-saṃghāta*); therefore, within the atom and the aggregate of atoms, there exists a characteristic that serves as the object-field (*viṣaya*) for the six consciousnesses.
The characteristic of an atom (*paramāṇu*) is not an object (*viṣaya*), just like solidity and so forth.

Within an atom there exist the tangibles of solidity, moisture, heat, and motion; these things truly exist, yet they are not the domain of visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), because visual consciousness does not arise with respect to them.
The atoms within all things are likewise so. Why is this?
If consciousness were to arise with respect to the atoms within all things, that consciousness would be without distinction, because there is no difference among the atoms within all things.

If you say that consciousness arises differently due to the distinction between characteristics—that is, because the appearances of various objects such as jars differ, and consciousness arises differently by taking those appearances as its object—then [we reply]:...
This argument is not tenable. Why?

Because such distinctions of appearance exist within conventionally designated objects like jars, but do not exist within substantial entities such as atoms (*paramāṇu*), for the essential dimension of an atom does not vary.

Among all phenomena, the dimension of the atom (paramāṇu) is spherical and subtle, without distinction; therefore, the characteristics of all phenomena do not exist substantially, but exist as mere designations (prajñapti).
That which is a conventional designation (*prajñapti-saṃjñā*) refers to things such as jars; for if one removes the atoms (*paramāṇu*), the cognition resembling a jar and so forth does not arise.

That which is a substantial entity (*dravya*) refers to that wherein, even if associated phenomena (*saṃprayukta-dharma*) are analyzed, the cognition resembling the substantial entity is not extinguished.

Just as when a jar has not yet been broken, the cognition of the five sense-objects arises within it, so too, once it has been broken, the cognition of the five sense-objects does not cease; therefore, the five sense-objects and so forth are substantially existent.
Because neither these atoms nor the aggregates of things can produce consciousness, external objects are not the objective domain of consciousness.
If this is so, what dharma is designated as an "object"?
The appearance of internal objects as if they were external is called the "object-condition of consciousness" (*vijñāna-viṣaya-pratyaya*).

External objects do not exist in reality; rather, because sentient beings have distracted minds within their internal consciousness, they give rise to the discrimination of the six sense-objects. This discrimination appears as if it were external, and among the four conditions, this is termed the "object-condition of consciousness. This is because it is the essential characteristic of that consciousness and because consciousness arises from it.

Why is this so? Because this consciousness produces the appearance of internal objects and arises from those internal objects; since it possesses these two characteristics, internal objects are called "objects of experience" (viṣaya).
Question: It may be granted that consciousness arises in dependence on external objects.
However, since internal objects are a part of consciousness itself and arise simultaneously with it, how can they function as an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*)?
Answer: Regarding the establishment of the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya), it is because consciousness arises conditioned by this [object], and there is no duality between them.
As for "condition," sometimes they arise simultaneously; it is that which can bring about other dharmas arising from another, as it invariably follows whether [the result] arises or does not arise.
Question:
If they arise in succession, what are the characteristics of the object-conditioned (ālambana) and the subject-conditioning (ālambaka)? Answer:

If the cause precedes and the effect follows, such that the effect conforms to the cause while the cause does not conform to the effect—wherein if the cause exists the effect necessarily exists, and if the cause is absent the effect necessarily is absent, and thus the existence or non-existence of the effect conforms to the cause—this is called the characteristic of cause and effect.
Furthermore, in order to establish the sequence of functional capacities, the object-condition (*ālambana*) and the subject-condition (*ālambaka*) are posited.

The sequential arising of consciousness that resembles the object is "arising" (*utpāda*); the arising of the capacity that resembles the fruit is the "arising of the continuity of consciousness" (*vijñāna-saṃtati-utpāda*).
Question: If the internal object (adhyātma-viṣaya) is consciousness and the objective condition (ālambana-pratyaya) is that which arises from conditions, how should the Sūtra explain this?
The Sūtra says, "Dependent upon the faculty (indriya) and conditioned by form (rūpa), eye-consciousness (cakṣurvijñāna) arises," as explained at length in the Sūtra.
Answer: That which possesses the functional capacity and essential characteristics to collectively produce a fruit is called a faculty (*indriya*).
Question:
What are the essence and function of the faculties (*indriya*)?
Answer:
Their essence consists of superior capacity.
By what means can this essence be inferred?
It is because it gives rise to its own effects; thus, its superior capacity can be discerned.
It is not that there are four great elements (mahābhūta) as form (rūpa), for this capacity exists within consciousness without any obstruction.
This capacity resides within consciousness; apart from consciousness, its essence cannot be demonstrated.
Since the sense faculties as I have established them and the sense faculties as you have established them both have this same capacity as their essence, what difference is there between them?
In this way, the functional capacity and the semblance of the object serve as mutual causes;

such functional capacities and semblances of objects have arisen in this manner from time immemorial. Based on the functional capacity, it is termed the "faculty" (*indriya*); based on the internal semblance of the object, it is termed the "object" (*viṣaya*).
This disordered consciousness (*vikṣipta-vijñāna*) cannot have its characteristics described; these dharmas arise such that they serve as mutual causes for one another, and there is no beginning.

Why is this? Because either the maturation of functional capacity gives rise to a consciousness resembling an object (*viṣaya*), or because of the consciousness resembling an object, the functional capacity is established.

Consciousness is either different from the two, not different from the two, or indescribable; thus, because the internal sense-object possesses these two qualities, it can serve as the objective domain of consciousness.
Treatise on the Non-Existence of Mental Objects Corresponding to Consciousness (Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra)
